The March 15, 2020 FOMC package (rate cut to the ELB, large-scale Treasury and agency MBS purchases, expanded repos, and coordinated dollar liquidity) directly targeted acute market-functioning and funding stresses and provided meaningful support to financial conditions. However, the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS) indicates a significant tightening in credit supply that will blunt transmission to the real economy.

Key SLOOS takeaways reinforcing a weaker near-term outlook:
- Banks tightened standards and other terms on C&I loans across firm sizes and on construction/land development and other CRE segments; medium-market firms also face tighter standards.
- Consumer credit tightened: higher credit score thresholds, reduced credit limits; some categories reported unchanged demand, but broader signals show weaker demand for certain loans (e.g., construction).
- Banks expect further tightening of lending standards in 2020, reduced risk tolerance, and deterioration in loan portfolios, collateral values, and HELOC performance.
- Expectations of deterioration extend to loans to small firms and syndicated loans, with multifamily CRE standards expected to tighten.

These SLOOS signals of tighter standards, higher borrower thresholds, and anticipated deterioration imply a contraction in credit availability just as the real economy faces simultaneous demand and supply shocks. While the Fed’s actions ease market dysfunction and dollar funding stress, the SLOOS evidence points to a more negative near-term growth and credit outlook than policy alone can offset.
